issues.legal_issue: A sale agreement is specifically enforceable where it is not contingent on the seller’s earlier purchase agreement, the seller later acquires transferable title and obtains the required permission, and the agreement obliges the seller to complete the steps necessary for conveyance.
material_facts: The seller agreed to sell the land and undertook to have it converted for non-agricultural use, obtain the conversion permission, and bear the related expenses.
The earlier owner’s application for conversion permission was rejected, but subsequent statutory changes extinguished that owner’s title and recognized the seller as an occupant of the land.
The seller obtained an occupancy certificate and later obtained permission to convert all of the land for non-agricultural use.
The sale agreement made conveyance follow conversion of the land; it did not make the seller’s obligations dependent on performance of the earlier purchase agreement.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was absolute and unconditional, not a contingent contract dependent on the earlier owner obtaining permission. Once the seller acquired transferable rights and obtained the required permission, there was no legal impediment to specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 31 and 32 of the Contract Act, a contract dependent on an uncertain event may be contingent, but the agreement here did not make performance dependent on the earlier owner’s success in obtaining permission. A vendor has an implied covenant to do what is necessary to give effect to the agreement, including obtaining required permission. Under section 13 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, a court may enforce the contract where the vendor’s later-acquired rights make transfer possible. Motilal v. Nanhelal Ghasiram, Mrs. Chandnee Widya Wati Madden v. Dr. C.L. Katial, and Ramesh Chandra Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal support the implied-covenant principle. Dalsukh M. Pancholi v. The Guarantee Life & Employment Insurance Company Ltd. was distinguishable because approval by the attaching court was an essential condition for both parties. F. Ranchhodas v. Natmal Hirachand & Co. was referred to on the timing of conveyance after permission.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A purchaser brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement to sell land.
predicates.sale_agreement_requires_conversion_befor: The agreement provided that conveyance would occur after the land was converted for the agreed use.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance suit concerns an agreement requiring conversion before conveyance, and the seller undertook to obtain permission, later acquired transferable occupancy rights, and obtained that permission, the agreement is specifically enforceable.

issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance is within the limitation period when it is brought within three years after the cause of action arises upon the conferral of occupancy rights and the grant of the required conversion permission.
material_facts: The seller was recognized as an occupant and received an occupancy certificate for the land.
The required conversion permission was granted for part of the land and later for the remaining part.
The purchaser filed the suit after the permissions had been obtained but within three years of the latest permission.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because it was filed within three years after the cause of action arose.
issues.legal_principle: Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1963 prescribes a three-year period for a suit for specific performance, running from the date the cause of action accrues. In this case, the cause of action arose after occupancy rights were conferred and the required conversion permission was obtained.
